settings.heading: What is road force balancing, and how does it work?
settings.body:
Road force balancing is a wheel balance plus a load test. A regular balancer spins the wheel in the air and finds the heavy spot. A road force balancer also presses a roller against the tread while the wheel turns, the way the road presses on a tire under the weight of your car, and measures how hard the tire pushes back all the way around.

That matters because no tire is perfectly uniform. The rubber is a little thicker here, the belts overlap there, one part of the sidewall is a touch stiffer. GM’s service bulletin on tire force variation puts it plainly: a perfectly balanced tire and wheel can still be slightly oval and cause a vibration. Weights can’t cancel that. Turning the tire on the rim to line up its stiff spot with the wheel’s low spot can.

The name comes from Hunter Engineering, which introduced a balancer with a simulated road test in 1997. In a chassis-dyno test described in Hunter’s 2004 balancer manual, about 30 lb of road force shook a test car as much as 1.5 oz (42 g) of wheel imbalance at 50 mph (about 80 km/h), and as much as 0.75 oz (21 g) at 70 mph (about 113 km/h). The same manual sets 0.30 oz as the limit for leftover imbalance, so at the lower speed that is five times the limit. It is why a car can feel rough on Deerfoot even when every wheel is balanced to the gram.

Our Edmonton Trail NE shop does it on a Hunter Road Force balancer, the type of machine the name comes from.

Road Force is a trademark of Hunter Engineering Company. Prince Tires uses Hunter equipment but is not otherwise affiliated with or endorsed by Hunter Engineering.

settings.heading: Signs you need a road force balance
settings.body:
Transport Canada notes that an out-of-balance wheel shows up as a pounding or shaking through the steering wheel or seat, and that it wears tires unevenly and shortens suspension life. A $20 standard balance is the first step. Ask for road force when:

  • It still shakes after a balance. The weights are right and the steering wheel still shimmies at 100 km/h on Deerfoot. GM names this exact complaint, a shake on smooth highway at about 105 to 115 km/h, as the most common sign of tire force variation.
  • A new set never rode smooth. Fresh tires should feel better than the old ones. If they don’t, one tire may have a stiff spot, and the readings show which one.
  • It started after a pothole. City crews filled 35,855 potholes in 2025, after a record 37,850 in 2024. A hit on McKnight, 16 Ave NE or Memorial Drive can leave a slightly bent rim without a mark you can see.
  • The shake moved after a rotation. If it went from the steering wheel to the seat, or the other way, when the tires swapped ends, the problem is travelling with a tire or wheel.

Shudder only when you brake? That’s almost always the brakes, not this. More on telling them apart: why your steering wheel shakes.

settings.heading: Who benefits most from road force balancing
settings.body:
• Low-profile tires and big wheels. Brake & Front End calls road force especially useful on very low-profile tires, where a short, stiff sidewall passes small flaws straight into the cabin. That covers most 19-inch and bigger wheel packages.
  • EVs. Not required, and we won’t tell you otherwise. But a quiet cabin makes vibration easier to notice, Continental lists load among the factors behind flat spots, and EVs are heavy. Tesla’s own service manual also includes a road force balance procedure.
  • Trucks on LT, all-terrain or 33- to 37-inch tires. Big, heavy tires are a common reason people ask for it. It isn’t required, and published limits for LT tires are looser than for passenger tires. Tell us the tire size when you request a time so we can confirm it fits our machine.
  • New tires you want right from day one. Optional. GM says this kind of machine shouldn’t be used to audit new tires, but matching a poor tire-and-wheel combination when the set goes on saves a trip back. Every tire installation already includes a standard balance; road force is the $15 per tire upgrade.
  • Tires just back from storage. After a spring or fall swap, a set that rode fine last season can shake for the first few kilometres. That’s usually a temporary flat spot, and Continental says it usually goes away in the first few kilometres of driving, once the tires reach operating temperature. Michelin says more than 20 minutes at highway speed relaxes most flat spotting. If the shake is still there after that, ask for the test.

settings.heading: What road force readings mean
settings.body:
Each wheel gets a road force reading, usually in pounds. Lower is smoother. There is no single pass mark that fits every car, because the limit depends on the vehicle and the tire. This is what has been published:

  • GM: 18 lb or less for passenger tires on cars, 24 lb for passenger tires on light trucks, 35 lb for LT tires. GM adds that some vehicles are more sensitive and need lower.
  • Hunter Engineering, 2004 balancer manual: default limits of 26 lb for passenger tires and 39 lb for LT tires, with a note that a very sensitive vehicle can react above 15 lb.
  • Tesla Model Y service manual: 125 N, about 28 lb.

We’ll show you each wheel’s number and what it means for your car. If a tire still reads high after match mounting, it may be a warranty question for the tire maker, and the reading helps make the case. The tire maker decides, though. Hunter’s manual says its limits shouldn’t be the only basis for replacing a tire, and GM warns that replacing tires below its limits will probably mean condemning good ones. See what tire warranties cover.

settings.heading: Match mounting: how road force can reduce a vibration
settings.body:
Most tires have a stiff spot and most wheels have a low spot. Match mounting turns the tire on the rim so the tire’s stiff spot sits at the wheel’s low spot, and the two partly offset each other instead of adding up. Tire and car makers have done the same thing at the factory for years.

To do it, the tire is partly dismounted, turned on the wheel and reseated. The TPMS sensor stays with the wheel. Then the assembly is balanced again, because moving the tire changes the balance; GM requires that step. A small amount of road force usually remains afterward, and that’s normal.

Sometimes a high reading is a mounting problem, not a bad tire. Hunter and GM both point to bead seating: a tire that didn’t seat evenly on the rim can read high, and remounting it with the right lubricant can bring the number down a long way. Tires may also carry factory marks for their high or light point, but brands don’t agree on what the colours mean, so we go by the measurement.

settings.heading: What road force balancing won’t fix
settings.body:
We’d rather tell you up front than take the job.

  • A pull to one side. Road force balancing is for vibration. A pull or uneven wear usually points to alignment, and Prince Tires doesn’t do wheel alignments, so you’ll need an alignment shop for that. A tire can cause a pull on its own, but a balance isn’t what fixes it.
  • Shudder under braking. Usually the brake rotors. Hunter’s 2004 balancer manual lists brake wear among the causes Hunter’s machine can’t detect.
  • Worn suspension, steering parts, wheel bearings or driveline. A worn ball joint or tie rod shows up as play, and a vibration that changes with engine speed rather than road speed is usually driveline. We don’t do mechanical repair.
  • Flat spots. They throw the reading off; road force doesn’t cure them. Driving does, if they’re temporary. Tires that sat loaded for a month or more can keep a semi-permanent flat spot.
  • A wheel bent too far. Match mounting can offset a small bend. A badly bent wheel needs repair or replacing, and we’ll show you the number so you can decide.

Michelin suggests having both alignment and balancing checked when you notice vibration, pulling or unsteady steering, and notes that cupped tread wear can come from worn shocks as well as imbalance. If the readings say it isn’t the tires or wheels, we’ll tell you so.

settings.question: What is road force balancing?
settings.answer: A road force balance is a standard wheel balance plus a load test. The balancer presses a roller against the tread as the wheel turns, the way the road does under your car, and measures how hard the tire pushes back. That can show stiff spots and out-of-round that a spin balance can’t measure. If a reading is high, we match mount: turn the tire on the rim so its stiff spot lines up with the wheel’s low spot, then balance it again.

settings.question: What’s the difference between road force balancing and a regular balance?
settings.answer: A regular (spin) balance only finds the heavy spot and corrects it with weights. Road force balancing does that too, then loads the tire with a roller to find stiff spots and out-of-round, and reduces them by match mounting. Start with a regular balance; road force is the next step when a vibration survives it.

settings.question: Is road force balancing worth it?
settings.answer: When a shake survives a regular balance, it’s the usual next step; that’s the job it’s built for. It can also be worth it on low-profile tires, 19-inch and bigger wheels, and heavy, quiet EVs where small flaws are easy to feel. It isn’t a gimmick, but it isn’t necessary on every car either. For an ordinary car with no vibration, a $20 standard balance is usually all you need, and we’ll tell you so.

settings.question: What road force number is good or acceptable?
settings.answer: There isn’t one number for every car. GM’s guide is 18 lb or less for passenger tires on cars and 35 lb for LT truck tires. Hunter’s 2004 balancer manual used 26 lb for passenger tires and 39 lb for LT tires, and noted a very sensitive car can react above 15 lb. Tesla lists 125 N (about 28 lb) for the Model Y. We’ll show you each wheel’s reading and what it means for your vehicle.

settings.question: Does road force balancing fix a pull or replace an alignment?
settings.answer: No. Road force balancing is for vibration. A pull to one side or uneven wear usually points to alignment, and Prince Tires doesn’t do wheel alignments. If your car pulls, we’ll tell you plainly that you need an alignment shop, not a balance.

settings.question: Will road force balancing fix flat spots?
settings.answer: No. Flat spots from a car sitting in the cold, or tires coming out of storage, make the reading come out high; they aren’t fixed by the machine. Temporary flat spots usually go away once the tires warm up, and Michelin says more than 20 minutes at highway speed relaxes most of them. Drive the car at highway speed on the way to your appointment so a temporary flat spot doesn’t throw the reading off.

settings.question: Can you road force balance truck tires, or 35- and 37-inch tires?
settings.answer: LT, all-terrain and mud-terrain truck tires are a common reason people ask for road force, and published limits for LT tires are looser than for passenger tires. Big tires have to fit the machine, so tell us the tire size and wheel size when you request a time and we’ll confirm before you come in. It’s optional, not required, for big tires.

settings.question: Do new tires need road force balancing?
settings.answer: Not usually. Every tire installation at Prince Tires includes a standard balance, and that’s enough for most cars. The road force upgrade ($15 per tire at Edmonton Trail NE) makes sense on low-profile tires, big wheels or an EV, or if you want a poor tire-and-wheel combination caught before you feel it.
